claim: Drosophila perform a body location-prioritized grooming sequence when mechanosensory neurons at different locations on the head and body are simultaneously stimulated by dust.
source: We previously discovered that Drosophila perform a body location-prioritized grooming sequence when mechanosensory neurons at different locations on the head and body are simultaneously stimulated by dust (Hampel et al., 2017; Seeds et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Hampel et al., 2017; Seeds et al., 2014)

claim: Nearly all mechanosensory neurons on the Drosophila head that individually elicit aimed grooming of specific head locations were identified.
source: Here, we identify nearly all mechanosensory neurons on the Drosophila head that individually elicit aimed grooming of specific head locations, while collectively eliciting a whole head grooming sequence.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including optogenetic activation experiments and anatomical reconstructions

claim: Different tracing methods were used to reconstruct the projections of head mechanosensory neurons from different locations on the head to their distinct arborizations in the brain.
source: Different tracing methods were used to reconstruct the projections of these neurons from different locations on the head to their distinct arborizations in the brain.
evidence: Supported by experimental methods described in the manuscript, including dye fills, transgenic driver lines, and EM reconstructions

claim: This work provides the first synaptic resolution somatotopic map of a head.
source: This provides the first synaptic resolution somatotopic map of a head, and defines the parallel-projecting mechanosensory pathways that elicit head grooming.
evidence: Supported by the comprehensive EM reconstruction data presented in the manuscript

claim: The parallel model proposes that premotor elements of different movements to be executed in sequence are activated in parallel and then selected sequentially through hierarchical suppression.
source: This model proposes that the premotor elements of different movements to be executed in sequence are activated (or readied) in parallel and then selected sequentially through a mechanism where movements occurring earlier in the sequence suppress later ones (Bohland et al., 2010; Bullock, 2004; Houghton and Hartley, 1995; Lashley, 1951).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on parallel models of movement sequences

claim: A hallmark feature of the parallel model is a parallel circuit architecture that ensures all mutually exclusive actions to be performed in sequence are simultaneously readied and competing for output.
source: A hallmark feature of this model is a parallel circuit architecture that ensures all mutually exclusive actions to be performed in sequence are simultaneously readied and competing for output.
evidence: Based on theoretical understanding of parallel models

claim: The parallel model architecture is supported by physiological and behavioral evidence from the movement sequences of different animals.
source: This architecture is supported by physiological and behavioral evidence from the movement sequences of different animals (Averbeck et al., 2002; Mushiake et al., 2006; Seeds et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Making flies dirty by coating them in dust elicits a grooming sequence that starts with the cleaning of different locations on the head and proceeds to body locations.
source: Making flies dirty by coating them in dust elicits a grooming sequence that starts with the cleaning of different locations on the head, such as the eyes, antennae, and proboscis, and proceeds to body locations, such as the abdomen, wings, and thorax (Mueller et al., 2019; Phillis et al., 1993; Seeds et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous behavioral studies

claim: The grooming sequence is produced by a mechanism consistent with a parallel model where different aimed grooming movements become activated in parallel by dust.
source: We previously determined that the sequence is produced by a mechanism that is consistent with a parallel model (Seeds et al., 2014). The sequence begins when different aimed grooming movements that clean specific locations of the head or body become activated in parallel by dust.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Seeds et al., 2014)

claim: Eye grooming occurs first in the sequence because eye grooming suppresses grooming of other locations on the head and body.
source: For example, grooming of the eyes occurs first because eye grooming suppresses grooming of other locations on the head and body.
evidence: Based on previous behavioral observations and the parallel model framework

claim: Tactile displacement of individual bristles elicits grooming movements in which the legs are precisely aimed at the stimulus location.
source: Tactile displacement of individual bristles elicits grooming movements in which the legs are precisely aimed at the stimulus location (Corfas and Dudai, 1989; Page and Matheson, 2004; Vandervorst and Ghysen, 1980).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Each bristle is innervated by a single bristle mechanosensory neuron (BMN) that is excited by displacement of that bristle.
source: Each bristle is innervated by a single bristle mechanosensory neuron (BMN) that is excited by displacement of that bristle (Corfas and Dudai, 1990; Tuthill and Wilson, 2016a; Walker et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Simultaneous optogenetic activation of mechanosensory neurons across the body elicits a grooming sequence that proceeds in the same order as the natural dust-induced sequence.
source: Simultaneous (parallel) optogenetic activation of mechanosensory neurons across the body elicits a grooming sequence that proceeds in the same order as the 'natural' dust-induced sequence (Hampel et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous optogenetic studies

claim: BMNs from different body locations show somatotopic organization in their CNS projections.
source: Previous studies of BMNs from different body locations demonstrated that they show somatotopic organization in their CNS projections (Johnson and Murphey, 1985; Murphey et al., 1989b; Newland, 1991; Newland et al., 2000; Tsubouchi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous anatomical studies

claim: Particular projection zones in the CNS correspond to specific body locations.
source: That is, particular projection zones in the CNS correspond to specific body locations.
evidence: Based on established understanding of somatotopic organization

claim: The antennal Johnston's organ (JO) is a chordotonal organ containing mechanosensory neurons called JO neurons (JONs) that detect stimulations of the antennae and elicit aimed grooming.
source: The antennal Johnston's organ (JO) is a chordotonal organ containing mechanosensory neurons called JO neurons (JONs) that detect stimulations of the antennae and elicit aimed grooming (Hampel et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Hampel et al., 2015)

claim: There are over 1000 bristles located on the head whose stimulation could elicit aimed grooming of different head locations.
source: There are over 1000 bristles located on the head whose stimulation we postulated could also elicit aimed grooming of different head locations.
evidence: Based on bristle counting data presented in the manuscript

claim: BMNs innervating bristles on the eyes elicit grooming of the eyes.
source: In support of this, BMNs innervating bristles on the eyes were previously shown to elicit grooming of the eyes (Hampel et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Activation of subsets of BMNs at other head locations elicits aimed grooming.
source: Here, we use optogenetic tools to show that activation of subsets of BMNs at other head locations also elicits aimed grooming.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: BMNs innervating neighboring head bristles project to overlapping zones in the CNS while those innervating distant bristles project to distinct zones.
source: This reveals somatotopic organization, where BMNs innervating neighboring head bristles project to overlapping zones in the CNS while those innervating distant bristles project to distinct zones.
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data presented in the manuscript

claim: Neighboring BMNs show higher connectivity similarity than distant BMNs.
source: Analysis of head BMN postsynaptic connectivity reveals that neighboring BMNs show higher connectivity similarity than distant BMNs, providing evidence of somatotopically organized postsynaptic circuit pathways.
evidence: Supported by connectomic analysis data presented in the manuscript

claim: Most of the bristles on the head were easily observed by imaging white light-illuminated heads.
source: Most of the bristles were easily observed by imaging white light-illuminated heads (Figure 1A–D), and color-coded depth maps further helped to distinguish between bristles while they were being counted (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–H).
evidence: Supported by imaging methods and figures showing bristle visualization

claim: R52A06-GAL4 labels almost all BMNs on the head, but does not label any associated with the postocellar (PoOc) or supracervical (Su) bristles.
source: R52A06-GAL4 labeled almost all BMNs on the head, but did not label any associated with the postocellar (PoOc) or supracervical (Su) bristles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–H).
evidence: Supported by transgenic expression pattern data

claim: BMNs innervating bristles at different locations on the head project through specific nerves, including the antennal, eye, occipital, and labial nerves.
source: This revealed that BMNs innervating bristles at different locations on the head project through specific nerves, including the antennal, eye, occipital, and labial nerves.
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data

claim: BMNs innervating the 18–22 antennal (Ant) bristles project through the antennal nerve (AntNv).
source: BMNs innervating the 18–22 antennal (Ant) bristles were previously reported to project through the antennal nerve (AntNv) that also carries the axons of JONs and olfactory neurons (Homberg et al., 1989; Melzig et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and data in the manuscript

claim: BMNs innervating frontal (Fr), orbital (Or), frontoorbital (FrOr), ocellar (Oc), interocellar (InOc), and some vibrissae (Vib) bristles project through the AntNv.
source: We identified additional BMNs projecting through the AntNv that innervate bristles located on the anterior and dorsal head (Figure 2E, I, blue). These include four to seven frontal (Fr) bristles located medially, three orbital (Or), and four to six frontoorbital (FrOr) bristles located laterally, and one ocellar (Oc) and three to four interocellar (InOc) bristles located on the dorsal head. BMNs projecting from these bristles form a bundle below the cuticle that projects ventrally to join the AntNv. We also identified BMNs that innervate one to three of the small anterior vibrissae (Vib) on the ventral head whose axons project dorsally to join the AntNv.
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data and figures

claim: BMNs innervating bristles on the dorsal half of the posterior head project through a previously undescribed nerve called the occipital nerve (OcciNv).
source: BMNs innervating bristles on the dorsal half of the posterior head project through a previously undescribed nerve that we named the occipital nerve (OcciNv) (Figure 2F and J, green).
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data and figures

claim: The OcciNv includes BMNs innervating the vertical (Vt), dorsal occipital (dOcci), and dorsal postorbital (dPoOr) bristles.
source: This includes the three to four vertical (Vt), two to five dorsal occipital (dOcci), and five to nine dorsal postorbital (dPoOr) bristles.
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data

claim: There are between 607 and 645 InOm bristles on each eye.
source: We estimated that there are between 607 and 645 InOm bristles on each eye based on published data (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on published data and calculations described in Materials and methods

claim: BMNs that innervate the InOm bristles form a nerve that projects to the brain from the posterior head called the eye nerve (EyeNv).
source: BMNs that innervate the InOm bristles were previously found to form a nerve that projects to the brain from the posterior head (Hampel et al., 2017). Because this nerve was not previously named, it is referred to here as the eye nerve (EyeNv).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and naming convention established in this study

claim: The EyeNv carries projections of BMNs innervating bristles on the posterior and ventral head, including ventral occipital (vOcci), ventral postorbital (vPoOr), and most vibrissae (Vib) bristles.
source: We found that the EyeNv also carries the projections of BMNs innervating bristles on the posterior and ventral head (Figure 2E–J, red). Those on the posterior head innervate the 12–18 ventral occipital (vOcci) and 9–15 ventral postorbital (vPoOr) bristles. Those on the ventral head innervate most of the 13–18 Vib bristles.
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data and figures

claim: BMNs innervating Taste bristles on the labellum project through the labial nerve (LabNv).
source: Each half of the labellum has 31–42 Taste bristles whose associated BMNs project through the labial nerve (LabNv) (Falk et al., 1976; Jeong et al., 2016; Nayak and Singh, 1983; Shanbhag et al., 2001; Stocker, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and data in the manuscript

claim: BMNs innervating the five haustellum (Hau) bristles project through the LabNv.
source: We found that BMNs innervating the five haustellum (Hau) bristles also project through the LabNv (Figure 2H and J, brown).
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data and figures

claim: BMNs innervating the 14–18 maxillary palp (MaPa) bristles project through the maxillary nerve (MaxNv).
source: BMNs that innervate the 14–18 maxillary palp (MaPa) bristles project through the maxillary nerve (MaxNv) that also carries the axons of olfactory neurons (Naresh Singh and Nayak, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and data in the manuscript

claim: The Lab- and MaxNvs merge as they approach the head.
source: The Lab- and MaxNvs merge as they approach the head, and in this work we refer to the merged nerve as the LabNv.
evidence: Supported by anatomical observations

claim: The LabNv merges with the EyeNv in the ventral head.
source: The LabNv then merges with the EyeNv in the ventral head, suggesting that these nerves project into the brain at the same location (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by anatomical observations and figures

claim: BMNs in the Ant-, Eye-, and LabNvs project into a region of the ventral brain called the subesophageal zone (SEZ).
source: BMNs in the Ant-, Eye-, and LabNvs were previously reported to project into a region of the ventral brain called the subesophageal zone (SEZ) (Figure 3A and B; Hampel et al., 2017; Jeong et al., 2016; Kamikouchi et al., 2006; Mitchell et al., 1999; Naresh Singh and Nayak, 1985; Stocker, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and data in the manuscript

claim: All head BMN nerves project into the SEZ.
source: We tentatively identified the OcciNv projecting into the SEZ from a lateral direction, revealing that all head BMN nerves project into the SEZ (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by anatomical observations and figures

claim: Most of the BMNs project into more ventral regions of the SEZ than the JONs.
source: Visualization of JONs and BMNs in the same expression pattern revealed that most of the BMNs project into more ventral regions of the SEZ than the JONs (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by anatomical observations and figures

claim: BMNs from different nerves project into distinct zones of the ventral SEZ.
source: Indeed, BMNs from different nerves were found to project into distinct zones of the ventral SEZ.
evidence: Supported by anatomical observations and computational alignment of expression patterns

claim: There are potential zones where overlap could occur between the projections of BMNs from different nerves.
source: However, we also observed potential zones where overlap could occur between the projections of BMNs from different nerves (discussed more below).
evidence: Based on anatomical observations

claim: Optogenetic activation of BMN types labeled by each driver line elicited grooming by the front legs that was aimed at specific head locations.
source: Optogenetic activation of BMN types labeled by each driver line elicited grooming by the front legs that was aimed at specific head locations (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic behavioral experiments and figures

claim: A driver line that expressed in different BMN types on the dorsal head elicited aimed dorsal head grooming.
source: For example, a line that expressed in different BMN types on the dorsal head elicited aimed dorsal head grooming (dBMN-spGAL4; BM-InOc, -Vt, and -dPoOr neurons, blue trace, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic behavioral experiments, figures, and videos

claim: BM-Taste neurons on the labellum elicited labellar grooming, but also grooming of neighboring locations on the proboscis and ventral head.
source: Indeed, BM-Taste neurons on the labellum elicited labellar grooming, but also grooming of neighboring locations on the proboscis and ventral head (TasteBMN-spGAL4, yellow trace includes proboscis and ventral head grooming, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic behavioral experiments, figures, and videos

claim: Activation of BM-InOm neurons elicited eye grooming, but also grooming of the neighboring dorsal head.
source: Activation of BM-InOm neurons (InOmBMN-LexA, Video 3) elicited eye grooming (red trace), but also grooming of the neighboring dorsal head (blue trace).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic behavioral experiments, figures, and videos

claim: Head BMNs elicit aimed grooming of their corresponding bristle locations, but also neighboring locations.
source: This suggested that head BMNs elicit aimed grooming of their corresponding bristle locations, but also neighboring locations.
evidence: Based on inference from optogenetic behavioral data

claim: Activation of BMNs on the posterior head elicited low levels of dorsal head grooming, but mostly a forward head nodding movement.
source: Activation of BMNs on the posterior head elicited low levels of dorsal head grooming (blue trace), but mostly a forward head nodding movement (Figure 9A–C, pBMN-spGAL4; BM-Vt, -dOcci, -dPoOr, and -vOcci neurons, Video 4).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic behavioral experiments, figures, and videos

claim: Nodding occurred in two different behavioral contexts: during dorsal head grooming and as an avoidance response.
source: This suggested that BMN-activated nodding occurs in two different behavioral contexts: during dorsal head grooming and as an avoidance response.
evidence: Based on inference from optogenetic behavioral observations

claim: Nodding-only movements are elicited by BM-dOcci and -vOcci neurons.
source: When taken together, our experiments suggest that nodding-only movements are elicited by BM-dOcci and -vOcci neurons and dorsal head grooming is elicited by BM-InOc, -Vt, -dPoOr, and -InOm neurons.
evidence: Based on inference from optogenetic behavioral data

claim: BMNs on the dorsal head and eyes elicited backward motions that appeared as if flies were avoiding something that touched the head.
source: In addition to grooming, BMNs on the dorsal head and eyes elicited backward motions that appeared as if flies were avoiding something that touched the head (dBMN-spGAL4 and InOmBMN-LexA).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic behavioral observations

claim: The backward motion and grooming were mutually exclusive and sequential, as the backward motion occurred transiently at the stimulus onset and was followed by grooming.
source: The backward motion and grooming were mutually exclusive and sequential, as the backward motion occurred transiently at the stimulus onset and was followed by grooming.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic behavioral observations

claim: The somatotopically organized head BMNs elicit both aimed grooming and avoidance-like responses.
source: Taken together, this study reveals that the somatotopically organized head BMNs elicit both aimed grooming and avoidance-like responses.
evidence: Based on synthesis of optogenetic behavioral data

claim: This work provides the most comprehensive definition of the BMNs for any body part of Drosophila (or any other insect).
source: This provides the most comprehensive definition of the BMNs for any body part of Drosophila (or any other insect), and an essential resource for future studies.
evidence: Based on the scope and completeness of the anatomical reconstructions presented

claim: Nearly all head BMNs were reconstructed in this work.
source: While nearly all head BMNs were reconstructed in this work, different knowledge gaps remain.
evidence: Based on the comprehensive reconstruction effort and validation against bristle counts

claim: It is unclear if the PoOc and Su bristles are innervated by BMNs.
source: First, it is unclear if the PoOc and Su bristles are innervated by BMNs because they could not be observed using transgenic driver lines or dye filling methods.
evidence: Based on negative results from experimental attempts

claim: One of the BM-Vt/PoOc neurons is proposed to innervate the PoOc bristle, based on proximity and presumed morphological similarity to neighboring BMNs.
source: We proposed that one of the BM-Vt/PoOc neurons innervates the PoOc bristle, based on proximity and presumed morphological similarity to the neighboring BM-Vt, -InOc, and -Oc neurons.
evidence: Based on inference from anatomical proximity and morphological similarity

claim: The Su bristles may be innervated by some of the 25 unknown sensory neurons reconstructed in this work.
source: For the Su bristles, one possibility is that they are innervated by some of the 25 unknown sensory neurons reconstructed in this work (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–Y).
evidence: Based on speculation about unidentified neurons

claim: The neurotransmitter predictions for the BMNs were overwhelmingly cholinergic.
source: Given that the neurotransmitter predictions for the BMNs were overwhelmingly cholinergic (not shown), and a previous study indicated that leg BMNs are sensitive to a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist (Tuthill and Wilson, 2016a), the parsimonious explanation is that the BMNs are cholinergic.
evidence: Based on machine learning predictions and citation to previous work

claim: The extent to which head BMNs use acetylcholine, histamine, or other neurotransmitters remains unresolved.
source: Thus, the extent to which head BMNs use acetylcholine, histamine, or other neurotransmitters remains unresolved.
evidence: Based on conflicting evidence from different studies

claim: The reconstruction and annotation of head mechanosensory neurons in FAFB provides an important resource for connectomics-based studies of mechanosensory processing.
source: The reconstruction and annotation of head mechanosensory neurons in FAFB provides an important resource for connectomics-based studies of mechanosensory processing (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on the value of the comprehensive dataset for future research

claim: The JONs, BMNs, and TPMNs project into distinct regions in the SEZ, showing modality-specific projections.
source: The reconstructed JONs, BMNs, and TPMNs project into distinct regions in the SEZ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and E), and therefore show modality-specific projections.
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data and figures

claim: The BMN projections are based on head location (somatotopic).
source: While the BMN projections are based on head location (somatotopic), the JON projections are based on mechanical stimulus modality, such as their responses to vibrational or tonic antennal movements (tonotopic) (Hampel et al., 2020a; Kamikouchi et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2020; Patella and Wilson, 2018).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data and citations to previous work

claim: There are potential overlapping projections between the most ventral projecting JONs (JO-F neurons) and some BMNs projecting through the AntNv.
source: However, there are potential overlapping projections between the most ventral projecting JONs (JO-F neurons) and some BMNs projecting through the AntNv (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on anatomical observations

claim: The JO-F neuron projections are somatotopic like the BMNs.
source: This overlap suggests that the JO-F neuron projections are somatotopic like the BMNs.
evidence: Based on inference from anatomical overlap

claim: Modality-specific mechanosensory projections are fundamental in insects.
source: Modality-specific mechanosensory projections are also reported in the VNC of Drosophila and other insects (e.g. BMNs, hair plates, campaniform sensilla, and chordotonal neurons), revealing this organization to be fundamental in insects (Merritt and Murphey, 1992; Murphey et al., 1989a; Phelps et al., 2021; Smith and Shepherd, 1996; Tsubouchi et al., 2017; Tuthill and Wilson, 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work across multiple insect species

claim: This work defines the somatotopic organization of the head BMNs.
source: This work defines the somatotopic organization of the head BMNs.
evidence: Based on the comprehensive anatomical reconstruction data presented

claim: Somatotopy was previously reported for BMNs innervating bristles on the bodies of Drosophila and other insects.
source: Somatotopy was previously reported for BMNs innervating bristles on the bodies of Drosophila and other insects (Johnson and Murphey, 1985; Murphey et al., 1989b; Newland, 1991; Newland et al., 2000; Tsubouchi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Previous studies only produced partial somatotopic maps using dye fills or transgenic driver lines.
source: However, these studies only produced partial somatotopic maps using dye fills or transgenic driver lines.
evidence: Based on assessment of previous literature

claim: There were no previous descriptions of somatotopy among the head BMNs.
source: Furthermore, there were no previous descriptions of somatotopy among the head BMNs.
evidence: Based on assessment of previous literature

claim: This work uses EM reconstructions to produce a comprehensive synaptic resolution somatotopic map of head BMNs in the same brain.
source: Here, we use EM reconstructions to produce a comprehensive synaptic resolution somatotopic map of head BMNs in the same brain.
evidence: Based on the EM reconstruction methods and data presented

claim: All reconstructed Drosophila head BMN types terminate their projections in the SEZ.
source: All reconstructed Drosophila head BMN types terminate their projections in the SEZ.
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data

claim: The first layers of BMN processing for the head occur in the SEZ.
source: This indicates that the first layers of BMN processing for the head occur in the SEZ.
evidence: Based on inference from anatomical data

claim: Head BMNs reported in other insects project into both the SEZ and thoracic ganglia.
source: In contrast, head BMNs reported in other insects project into both the SEZ and thoracic ganglia, including BMNs innervating the InOm bristles of the praying mantis and cricket (Honegger, 1977; Zack and Bacon, 1981) and wind-sensitive head bristles of the locust (Tyrer et al., 1979).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work in other insect species

claim: Head BMNs that innervate the same bristle populations project into the same zones in the SEZ and show the highest morphological similarity.
source: Head BMNs that innervate the same bristle populations (same types) project into the same zones in the SEZ, show the highest morphological similarity, and their morphology is stereotyped across individual flies.
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data from multiple individuals

claim: The stereotyped projections of BMNs innervating specific bristles likely apply to most BMNs.
source: These characteristics likely apply to most BMNs, as numerous studies have identified the stereotyped projections of BMNs innervating specific bristles on the bodies of Drosophila and other insects (Burg and Wu, 1986; Burg and Wu, 1989; Burg et al., 1993; Chen et al., 2006; Ghysen, 1980; Honegger, 1977; Kays et al., 2014; Murphey et al., 1989b; Zack and Bacon, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work across multiple species

claim: Head BMNs of the same type show the highest postsynaptic connectivity similarity.
source: Head BMNs of the same type also show the highest postsynaptic connectivity similarity.
evidence: Supported by connectomic analysis data

claim: Some BMN types fall into multiple different NBLAST and cosine similarity clusters, revealing that there are BMN subtypes with differing morphology and postsynaptic connectivity.
source: However, some BMN types fall into multiple different NBLAST and cosine similarity clusters, revealing that there are BMN subtypes with differing morphology and postsynaptic connectivity.
evidence: Supported by NBLAST and connectomic analysis data

claim: The BM-InOm neurons show differential clustering, which could reflect the large surface area of the eyes that spans from the dorsal to ventral head.
source: One notable example of such intratype diversity are the BM-InOm neurons that show differential clustering (Figure 8—figure supplement 3). This could reflect the large surface area of the eyes that spans from the dorsal to ventral head, and the differentially clustered BM-InOm neurons may innervate bristles at different locations on the eyes.
evidence: Based on inference from clustering analysis and anatomical considerations

claim: BMN types innervating neighboring bristle populations have overlapping projections into zones that correspond roughly to the dorsal, ventral, and posterior head.
source: We also find that BMN types innervating neighboring bristle populations have overlapping projections (example shown in Figure 8E) into zones that correspond roughly to the dorsal, ventral, and posterior head.
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data and figures

claim: The overlap between neighboring BMN types is likely functionally significant, as cosine similarity analysis revealed that neighboring head BMN types can have common postsynaptic partners.
source: The overlap is likely functionally significant, as cosine similarity analysis revealed that neighboring head BMN types can have common postsynaptic partners (example shown in Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by connectomic analysis data and figures

claim: Overlap between neighboring BMN types is only partial, as they show differing projections and postsynaptic connectivity.
source: However, overlap between neighboring BMN types is only partial, as they show differing projections and postsynaptic connectivity.
evidence: Supported by anatomical and connectomic data

claim: The extent of overlap likely reflects the proximity between bristles and enables postsynaptic partners to respond to mechanosensory stimulations of neighboring bristles whose corresponding BMNs are likely to show correlated activity.
source: The extent of overlap likely reflects the proximity between bristles and enables postsynaptic partners to respond to mechanosensory stimulations of neighboring bristles whose corresponding BMNs are likely to show correlated activity (Tuthill and Wilson, 2016b).
evidence: Based on inference from anatomical and connectomic data, with citation to previous work

claim: BMN projection overlap has also been observed with other parts of the body in Drosophila.
source: BMN projection overlap has also been observed with other parts of the body in Drosophila.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: BMNs innervating bristles on the anterior and posterior leg compartments show overlapping projections in the VNC leg neuromere anterior and posterior zones, respectively.
source: For example, BMNs innervating bristles on the anterior and posterior leg compartments show overlapping projections in the VNC leg neuromere anterior and posterior zones, respectively (Murphey et al., 1989b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: BMNs innervating neighboring bristles on the thorax show overlap in their projections into the accessory mesothoracic neuropil.
source: Similarly, BMNs innervating neighboring bristles on the thorax show overlap in their projections into the accessory mesothoracic neuropil (Ghysen, 1980; Kays et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Neighboring BMNs could connect with common neural circuits to elicit grooming of overlapping locations.
source: This overlap may have implications for aimed grooming behavior. For example, neighboring BMNs could connect with common neural circuits to elicit grooming of overlapping locations (discussed more below).
evidence: Based on speculation about functional implications

claim: Some head BMNs have projections that remain in the ipsilateral brain hemisphere, while others have midline-crossing projections to the contralateral hemisphere.
source: The somatotopic map reveals that some head BMNs have projections that remain in the ipsilateral brain hemisphere, while others have midline-crossing projections to the contralateral hemisphere (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data and figures

claim: BMNs innervating bristles located medially on the anterior head show midline-crossing projections, whereas those innervating more lateral populations have ipsilateral-only projections.
source: Interestingly, BMNs innervating bristles located medially on the anterior head show midline-crossing projections, whereas those innervating more lateral populations have ipsilateral-only projections.
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data

claim: BMNs innervating medial bristles on the thorax have midline-crossing projections, while those innervating more lateral bristles have ipsilateral-only projections.
source: Previous studies found that BMNs innervating medial bristles on the thorax have midline-crossing projections, while those innervating more lateral bristles have ipsilateral-only projections (Ghysen, 1980; Kays et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: BMNs that innervate bristles located on the leg segment most medial to the body (coxa) have midline-crossing projections.
source: Similarly, BMNs that innervate bristles located on the leg segment most medial to the body (coxa) have midline-crossing projections (Murphey et al., 1989b; Phelps et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work
